title: City police officers cleared in 2016 remand centre death
article: An investigation into the 2016 death of a man in custody has determined two Winnipeg officers involved in the incident will not face charges, the province's police watchdog says.

Russell Spence, 31, died of a heart problem "magnified by the toxic effects of methamphetamine" after a struggle with two police officers and three corrections officers in a shower room at the Winnipeg Remand Centre, the Independent Investigation Unit of Manitoba (IIU) said in releasing its report Friday.
The IIU investigates all serious incidents involving on- or off-duty police in the province.
Spence was arrested without incident while holding a knife at an Ellice Avenue convenience store in October 2016. A witness said Spence had asked bystanders to call the police.

On the way to the remand centre, Spence was banging his head against the wall of the police van, another prisoner in the van told IIU investigators. Spence asked police to beat him, the prisoner said.

Inside the shower room at the centre, an altercation began between Spence and three corrections officers, a corrections officer who was in the room told investigators. Although the IIU reviewed the centre's security camera footage, there are no cameras in the room, the report says.
Audio transcripts obtained by the IIU show there was shouting coming from the room, drawing the police officers inside.

A corrections officer who also entered the room told the IIU they saw three corrections officers and two police officers restraining the naked Spence, who was resisting them. They didn't see the two police officers hit, punch or kick the man, the report says.
At some point, Spence's heart stopped, and he was taken to the Health Sciences Centre, where he was pronounced dead.

A pathologist determined the cause of death was cardiac arrhythmia (abnormal heart rhythm) made worse by the methamphetamine in his system "combined with the stress and injuries he incurred from being involved in a physical altercation," the IIU said. Spence also had a slightly enlarged heart.
The pathologist found no evidence a Taser had been used, the IIU said.
Manitoba's chief medical examiner has called for an inquest into Spence's death.
Also Friday, the IIU announced RCMP did not use excessive or unnecessary force when removing an intoxicated man from a home in Thompson in March.

In his report on the incident, IIU civilian director Zane Tessler said when one officer tried to handcuff the man, he was only able to get the cuff onto one wrist. The man assaulted the officer and tried to flee from the home.
He was bleeding from the head and had no shoes on, said a witness who had called the police.
Other officers tried to stop him as he fled, but the man struck one on the head with the handcuffs.
Police took him to the ground but he kept fighting, Tessler wrote. After his arrest, the man was taken to the hospital, where medical staff determined he had a broken rib.
The man told IIU investigators he had little memory of the incident - he told them he drank rye, vodka and beer, and ingested some cocaine that day.
He told investigators he remembered hiding behind a dumpster, and police telling him to come out, and later being in a police vehicle.

A civilian witness told police she called for them because he showed up at her house drunk, started banging on the door and arguing with her. She told investigators she saw police repeatedly punch the man in the head and kick him in the back.

However, Tessler found in his report that police hadn't used excessive or unnecessary force. The suspect refused to be handcuffed, was combative with police, and the officers stopped using physical force once he stopped resisting, Tessler wrote.
For the report, the IIU interviewed the man whose rib was broken, two civilian witnesses and identified seven witness RCMP officers.
The IIU determined no officers should face charges for the incident.
